Dimensionality reduction is a machine learning technique that reduces the number of input variables (features) in a dataset while retaining essential information and patterns.

The data used in this project is about the crimes committed between years 2003-2019 in the Republic of Ireland. The data was obtained from kaggle."This data set in its original form has been taken from StatBank, Central Statistics Office, Govt. of Ireland website - \> <https://statbank.cso.ie/>"

# Loading the libraries and reading the data set

```{r}

library(tidyverse)   
library(factoextra)  
library(cluster)
library(gridExtra)
library(Rtsne)       
library(corrplot)     
library(ggrepel)  
library(ggfortify)


crime_data <- read.csv("IRELAND_CRIME_GARDA_DIVISION_wise_2003-2019.csv", check.names = FALSE)
#View(crime_data)

```

# Identifying the quarters' columns

```{r}
quarter_cols <- colnames(crime_data)[6:ncol(crime_data)]

quarter_cols
```

# Initial Analysis of dataset

We calculate the total crimes per offence type for each Garda division and reshape the data into a wide matrix ready for analysis

```{r}
str(crime_data)

crime_data$Total_Crimes <- rowSums(crime_data[quarter_cols], na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#Mean of the for the total crimes committed.

mean(crime_data$Total_Crimes, na.rm = TRUE)

names(crime_data)
```

```{r}
# We keep only needed columns
crime_clean <- crime_data[, c("GARDA DIVISION", "TYPE OF OFFENCE", "Total_Crimes")]

# Aggregate totals by Division and Offence Type
crime_clean <- aggregate(
  Total_Crimes ~ `GARDA DIVISION` + `TYPE OF OFFENCE`,
  data = crime_clean,
  sum
)

# We convert from long to wide format
crime_clean <- reshape(
  crime_clean,
  idvar = "GARDA DIVISION",
  timevar = "TYPE OF OFFENCE",
  direction = "wide"
)

# Fix column names 
colnames(crime_clean) <- sub("Total_Crimes\\.", "", colnames(crime_clean))

# Set row names as divisions
rownames(crime_clean) <- crime_clean$`GARDA DIVISION`
crime_clean$`GARDA DIVISION` <- NULL
```

```{r}

# We ask ourselves do certain crimes happen together?

data_corr <- cor(crime_clean, method="pearson") 
corrplot(data_corr, order ="alphabet", tl.cex=0.3)

# The correlation matrix shows strong positive correlations among most crime categories, 
# indicating substantial shared variance and redundancy in the data. 

```

```{r}
#Summary of the data and a plot

summary(crime_data)

plot(crime_clean[,1])
```

#Principal Component Analysis (PCA) PCA is an unsupervised, dimensionality reduction technique that transforms large, correlated datasets into a smaller, uncorrelated set of variables called principal components, retaining maximum variance. Below we perform PCA on our scaled data.

```{r}
crime_numeric <- crime_data[, sapply(crime_data, is.numeric)]
```

```{r}

pca_crime <- prcomp(crime_numeric, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

summary(pca_crime)
```

#The scree plot shows a clear elbow after the second component, indicating that #the first two principal components capture most of the variance.

```{r}
var_explained <- pca_crime$sdev^2 / sum(pca_crime$sdev^2)

plot(
  var_explained,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "Principal Component",
  ylab = "Proportion of Variance Explained"
)
```

```{r}
# Cumulative variance

plot(
  cumsum(var_explained),
  type = "b",
  xlab = "Principal Component",
  ylab = "Cumulative Proportion of Variance"
)
abline(h = 0.85, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

```{r}
ggplot(loadings, aes(PC1, PC2, label = variable)) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(xend = 0, yend = 0),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm")),
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  geom_text(hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.1, colour = "red") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "PCA Loadings Plot"
  )
```

```{r}

# Biplot
fviz_pca_biplot(pca_crime, repel = TRUE, col.var = "red")

#The biplot shows that most crime categories load positively on PC1,
#consistent with an overall crime intensity factor.

autoplot(
  pca_crime,
  loadings = TRUE,
  loadings.label = TRUE)

```

# Clustering

Clustering is an unsupervised machine learning technique that automatically groups similar data points into clusters based on shared characteristics, without requiring pre-existing labels

Before we proceed, we take a look at different number of clusters and plot them.

```{r}

crime_scaled <- scale(crime_numeric)

k1 = kmeans(crime_scaled, centers=2, nstart=25)
k2 = kmeans(crime_scaled, centers=3, nstart=25)
k3 = kmeans(crime_scaled, centers=4, nstart=25)
k4 = kmeans(crime_scaled, centers=5, nstart=25)


p1 <- fviz_cluster(k1, geom = "point", crime_scaled) + ggtitle("k = 2")
p2 <- fviz_cluster(k2, geom = "point", crime_scaled) + ggtitle("k = 3")
p3 <- fviz_cluster(k3, geom = "point", crime_scaled) + ggtitle("k = 4")
p4 <- fviz_cluster(k4, geom = "point", crime_scaled) + ggtitle("k = 5")

grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, nrow=2)
```

```{r}
#We find optimal number of clusters below - Elbow method

fviz_nbclust(crime_scaled, kmeans, method = "wss") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = 2, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Elbow Method for Optimal K",
       subtitle = "Looking for the 'bend' in the curve",
       x = "Number of Clusters (k)",
       y = "Total Within-cluster Sum of Squares")
```

```{r}
#Silhouette method

fviz_nbclust(crime_scaled, FUN = kmeans, method = "silhouette")

#Visualisation
sil<-silhouette(k3$cluster, dist(crime_scaled))
fviz_silhouette(sil)
```

K-Means was selected as the primary clustering algorithm due to its interpretability and its ability to define Centroid-based profiles.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
km_crime <- kmeans(crime_scaled, centers = 2, nstart = 25)
km_crime1 <- kmeans(crime_scaled, centers = 3, nstart = 25)


fviz_cluster(km_crime, data = crime_scaled, palette = "viridis", ggtheme = theme_minimal())
fviz_cluster(km_crime1, data = crime_scaled, palette = "viridis", ggtheme = theme_minimal())


plot(crime_scaled, col = crime_data$`OFFENCE CODE`, pch=".", cex=3)
```

The k-means clustering with k = 2 separates divisions primarily along the first principal component, which explains 75.7% of the variance and represents overall crime intensity. Cluster 1 contains divisions with consistently higher crime levels across most categories, including major urban and metropolitan areas. Cluster 2 consists of divisions with lower and more homogeneous crime levels. The second component explains relatively little variance, indicating that differences in crime composition play a secondary role in the clustering.

```{r}
# Hierarchical clustering - This depicts the "genetic" relationship between divisions.

# We perform the GAP stat to give us optimal number of K 
gap_stat <- clusGap(crime_scaled, FUN = kmeans, nstart = 25, K.max = 10, B = 50)
fviz_gap_stat(gap_stat)

# Dendrogram
dist_mat <- dist(crime_scaled, method = "euclidean")
h_clust <- hclust(dist_mat, method = "ward.D2")
plot(h_clust, cex = 0.7, main = "Dendrogram of Crime Similarity")

#If two divisions merge early (at a low height), they share a similar economic structure. For example, 
#if two mid-sized towns merge, it suggests they face similar socio-economic challenges regardless of 
#their physical distance.
```
